units.title: The Cold War
units.intro: Not a direct US–USSR shooting war. It was a global contest of systems: capitalism + liberal democracy vs communism + one-party state, fought with alliances, aid, spies, local wars, the arms race and the space race.

f1.title: Europe split first. Berlin sat inside the Soviet zone — and was itself split.

cards.title: 1.1 Development of the cold war
body: The longstanding distrust and suspicions, which had been building up between the Soviet Union and the West (America, Britain, France and their allies) started to resurface even before the total victory of the allies.
One immediate issue of contention between the Soviet Union and the West was the fate of Eastern Europe.
The Western powers, which had once believed that the Soviets were in a weak position, were now faced with the reality of a strong Soviet army taking possession of Eastern and much of Central Europe.
The United States demanded popular elections throughout Eastern Europe.
Unit 1 The Cold War experience in the Second World War and having lost more people than any other country in the war, the Soviet Union sought absolute military security.

cards.title: Europe split first. Berlin sat inside the Soviet zone — and was itself split.
How it started
body:
- 1945: WWII ends; wartime allies already disagree over Eastern Europe. Stalin keeps the Red Army there and installs friendly governments.
- 1947 **Truman Doctrine**: US money to states threatened by communist expansion (starts with Greece after Britain pulls out).
- 1947 **Marshall Plan**: ~＄13 billion to rebuild Western Europe so poverty would not feed revolution. USSR answers with **COMECON** (little cash behind it).
- US policy name: **containment** — hold communism where it already is.

cards.title: Memory chain
body: Yalta/Potsdam distrust → Truman Doctrine → Marshall Plan → two Germanies / two Berlins → NATO (1949) vs Warsaw Pact (1955).

cards.title: How it ended
head: Date
Event
rows: — economic stagnation, Afghan war drain, arms-race cost.
— *perestroika* (rebuild the economy) and *glasnost* (openness). He does not send tanks when Eastern Europe rises.
— revolutions; Berlin Wall opens; 1990 Germany reunifies.
— failed hard-line coup; Soviet Union dissolves. Yugoslavia then breaks up in nationalist wars.

cards.title: How it ended
body: Science race: nuclear weapons, ICBMs, satellites, 1969 Moon landing — prestige as much as security.

cards.title: Sticky wall
body: 1947 Truman + Marshall 1949 NATO · 1955 Warsaw 1961 Wall · 1962 Cuba 1989–91 endgame

cards.title: The Marshall Plan and the Soviet answer (COMECON)
body: **Step 1 – what it was.** In June 1947, right after the Truman Doctrine, US Secretary of State **George C. Marshall** proposed the **European Recovery Program**, better known as the Marshall Plan.
**Step 2 – what it gave.** About **$13 billion** in aid to rebuild the war-damaged economies of Europe.

**Step 3 – why the USA did it.** Americans believed communist revolutions succeed where people are poor and economies are in crisis. Rebuilding Europe's economy would take away that chance, so the plan was part of **containment**.
**Step 4 – how the Soviets saw it.** The USSR saw the plan as an attempt to **buy the support of European countries** and kept Eastern Europe out of it.

**Step 5 – the Soviet reply.** In **1949** the USSR founded the **Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (COMECON)** for Eastern European states. COMECON largely failed because the Soviet Union could not provide enough money.
**Memory trick:** "Truman promised, Marshall paid, Moscow answered with COMECON."
**Exam tip:** If asked for the main aim of the Marshall Plan, answer "to rebuild Western Europe's economy so that communism could not spread" – both halves earn marks.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “The search for security during the Cold War led to the formation of new military alliances (NATO in the West, the Warsaw Pact in the East).”

**Step 2:** **Bulgaria** was a member of the **Warsaw Pact**, which was the military alliance of the Eastern Bloc led by the Soviet Union, created to oppose NATO.

**Step 3:** So the answer is C) Bulgaria.

**Tip:** Underline the key word in the question (true / not / except / first / last), then test every option against the lesson facts and dates.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** From the lesson: “East Germany seals the border to stop people leaving. Concrete symbol of the split until 1989.”

**Step 2:** **Step 1:** Identify the timeline. The Berlin Wall was built in August 1961.
**Step 2:** Determine the Soviet leader in 1961. **Nikita Khrushchev** was the Premier of the Soviet Union at that time.
**Step 3:** Khrushchev authorized the East German government to build the wall to stop the mass exodus of people to West Berlin.
**Result:** Khrushchev.

**Step 3:** So the answer is A) Khrushchev.

cards.title: Model answer: how the Cold War began
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the causes of the Cold War after the Second World War.

steps.text: Long-term cause: distrust and suspicion between the Soviet Union and the West (America, Britain, France) that resurfaced even before the allies' final victory.
Immediate issue: the fate of Eastern Europe – the Red Army stayed there and Stalin installed friendly governments, while the USA demanded popular elections.
The Soviet view: having lost more people than any other country, the USSR sought absolute military security.

The US answer (1947): the Truman Doctrine (money to states threatened by communist expansion, starting with Greece) and the Marshall Plan (about $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe); the USSR answered with COMECON.
Name the policy: containment – hold communism where it already is.

cards.answer: Mutual distrust plus the quarrel over Eastern Europe led to rival policies – Soviet security buffer vs US containment (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan) – which split Europe into two blocs.

lessons.title: The Spread of the Cold War

cards.title: 1.2 The Spread of the Cold War
body: Soon, the United States and the Soviet Union were involved in a growing arms race, in which both countries built up their armies and weapons.
The search for security during the Cold War led to the formation of new military alliances.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) was formed in April 1949 when Belgium, Luxembourg, France, the Netherlands, Great Britain, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, and Iceland signed a treaty with the United States and Canada.
All these powers agreed to provide military support if any one of them was attacked.
New military alliances spread to the rest of the world after the United States became involved in the Korean War (see next unit).

cards.title: It goes global · Alliances
body: NATO in the west. Warsaw Pact in the east. Arms race: A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles.

cards.title: Berlin Wall 1961
body: East Germany seals the border to stop people leaving. Concrete symbol of the split until 1989.

cards.title: Korea 1950–53
body: North (backed by USSR/China) vs South (UN/US). Ends near the 38th parallel. UN action happened while the USSR was boycotting the Security Council.

cards.title: Cuba 1962
body: Soviet missiles on the island. Closest brush with nuclear war. Deal: missiles out of Cuba; later US missiles out of Turkey; promise not to invade Cuba.

cards.title: Vietnam
body: Domino theory: if one state falls, neighbours follow. Long US war, huge anti-war movement at home, communist victory in 1975.

cards.title: Suez 1956
body: Nasser nationalises the canal. Britain, France, Israel attack; US and USSR both pressure them to stop. Nasser’s prestige rises. United Arab Republic with Syria is short-lived (Syria leaves 1961).

cards.title: It goes global
body: **Non-Aligned Movement:** newly independent states (Nehru, Nasser, Tito, later many Africans) refuse to be a US or Soviet satellite.
**UN:** born 1945 to keep peace. Cold War often froze the Security Council with vetoes. Still a stage for debate, agencies and rare joint action.

cards.title: Why Nasser's foreign policy angered the West
body: **Step 1 – background.** In **1952** army officers overthrew the Egyptian monarchy. Under **Gamal Abdel Nasser** the new government wanted to modernize Egypt, develop the economy and control the Suez Canal. He negotiated loans from the USA, Britain and the World Bank for the **Aswan High Dam**.

**Step 2 – the four policies that alarmed the West.** (1) open support for anti-colonial movements in **Kenya and Algeria**; (2) an **arms deal with communist Czechoslovakia**; (3) attending the **Bandung Conference (1955)** and co-founding the **Non-Aligned Movement**; (4) formal **recognition of the People's Republic of China**.
**Step 3 – the result.** The West cancelled the loans. Nasser **nationalized the Suez Canal (1956)** to pay for the dam, and Britain, France and Israel attacked Egypt – the **Suez Crisis**.
**Memory trick – "K-A-C-B-C":** Kenya and Algeria, Czech arms, Bandung, China.
**Exam tip:** When the answer choices list several of these policies, the correct option is usually "all of the above".

**Step 2:** **Austria** is a neutral country and is not a member of NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization). Belgium, France, Denmark, and Norway were all founding members or early joiners of the alliance.

cards.title: Model answer: the Cuban Missile Crisis
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why is the Cuban Missile Crisis seen as the most dangerous moment of the Cold War, and how was it solved?

steps.text: What happened: the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles on the island of Cuba, close to the USA.
Why dangerous: it was the closest brush with nuclear war in the arms race (A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles).
The deal: Soviet missiles were taken out of Cuba; later US missiles were taken out of Turkey; the USA promised not to invade Cuba.
Link to the theme: it shows how the arms race spread the Cold War beyond Europe.

cards.answer: Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers to the edge of nuclear war; it ended with a deal – missiles out of Cuba, later US missiles out of Turkey and a US promise not to invade Cuba.

lessons.title: United Nations Organization and the Cold war

cards.title: 1.3 United Nations Organization and the Cold war
body: The United Nations Organization (UNO) was established immediately after the end of the Second World War.
The founders of the UN believed that future disputes between countries could be settled by discussion, conciliation and arbitration.
Member states could be called upon to make troops available for peacekeeping missions.
Representatives of all states belonging to the UN meet at least once a year in New York for the General Assembly.
The five permanent members of the Security Council (the USA, USSR, Britain, France and China) have a privileged position compared to other member states.

cards.title: Model answer: the UN and the Cold War
cards.problem: (Short answer) Explain how the United Nations was organised to keep peace and why the Cold War limited it.

steps.text: Founding idea: the UN was set up right after the Second World War; its founders believed disputes could be settled by discussion, conciliation and arbitration.
General Assembly: all member states meet at least once a year in New York.
Security Council: five permanent members (USA, USSR, Britain, France, China) have a privileged position; member states can be asked to provide troops for peacekeeping.
Cold War limit: the two rival superpowers both sat as permanent members, so they could block each other (in Korea the UN acted only because the USSR was boycotting the Security Council).

cards.answer: The UN works through the General Assembly and the Security Council, but superpower rivalry among the permanent five often paralysed it during the Cold War.

lessons.title: Domestic Developments within the Eastern and Western blocs

cards.title: 1.4 Domestic Developments within the Eastern and Western blocs
body: During the Second World War the Soviet Union was devastated. 25 million of its citizens perished and its economy was destroyed.
To create a new industrial base, therefore, Stalin returned to the method that he had used in the 1930s.
Soviet workers were expected to produce goods for export with little reward.
The incoming capital from abroad could then be used to buy machinery and Western technology.
Economic recovery in the Soviet Union was spectacular.

cards.title: Inside each bloc
body: East: Soviet control, 1956 Hungary and 1968 Czechoslovakia crushed when they stray. West: reconstruction, welfare states, youth revolt in the 1960s, US civil rights and Vietnam protests.

cards.title: Fear of communism at home and the closest nuclear scare
body: **Step 1 – the Red Scare at home.** In the early 1950s Cold War tensions abroad caused widespread fear in the USA that communists had secretly entered American life. Truman's attorney general warned that communists were "everywhere".

**Step 2 – McCarthy.** The main agitator was **Senator Joseph R. McCarthy**, who claimed that large numbers of communists and Soviet spies worked inside the US government. His charges created a massive **"Red Scare"** – fear of communist subversion. Intellectuals and film stars were questioned about communist activities. When he attacked alleged "conspirators" in the US Army, the **Senate condemned him in 1954**.

**Step 3 – the closest nuclear scare abroad.** The real brink of nuclear war came with the **Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962)**. After Castro's revolution (1959) and the failed CIA-backed **Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961)**, the USSR began placing nuclear missiles in Cuba.

**Step 4 – how it ended.** The USA blockaded Cuba. **Khrushchev** turned his ships back and removed the missiles in return for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and the USA secretly removed its missiles from Turkey. A **hotline** between the Kremlin and the White House was then set up.
**Memory trick:** "McCarthy scared America; Cuba scared the world."
**Exam tip:** Questions about the "closest nuclear scare" always mean the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, not the Red Scare.

cards.title: The Prague Spring (1968)
body: **Step 1 – the reforms.** In **January 1968** the Czechoslovak government introduced reforms: freedom of speech and press, freedom to travel abroad, relaxed censorship, a more independent foreign policy and a promise of gradual democratization.
**Step 2 – the name.** The hopeful mood that followed was called the **"Prague Spring"**.
**Step 3 – the end.** The **Soviet army invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968** and crushed the reform movement.

**Step 4 – compare Hungary (1956).** Twelve years earlier the Soviet army attacked Budapest after Hungary announced it would leave the Warsaw Pact. Both cases show the USSR would not allow its satellites to leave its control.
**Memory trick:** "Hungary 56, Prague 68 – tanks both times."
**Exam tip:** The East European country invaded by the Soviets in 1968 is Czechoslovakia; in 1956 it was Hungary.

cards.title: Model answer: life in the two blocs
cards.problem: (Exam question) Compare domestic developments in the Eastern and Western blocs after 1945.

steps.text: East – recovery: the USSR (25 million dead) rebuilt with Stalin's 1930s methods: exports with little reward for workers, capital spent on Western machinery – spectacular recovery.
East – control: Soviet control of Eastern Europe; Hungary (1956) and Czechoslovakia (1968) crushed when they strayed.
West – recovery: reconstruction and welfare states.
West – protest: youth revolt in the 1960s, US civil rights and anti-Vietnam War protests.

cards.answer: Both blocs recovered fast, but the East was rebuilt under tight Soviet control (crushing Hungary 1956, Czechoslovakia 1968) while the West built welfare states and allowed open protest movements.

lessons.title: From Cold War to Post-Cold War

cards.title: 1.5 From Cold War to Post-Cold War
body: By the 1970s, American-Soviet relations had entered a new phase, known as détente, which was marked by a relaxation of tensions and improved relations between the two superpowers.
Beginning in 1979, however, the apparent collapse of détente began a new period of East-West confrontation.
The American-Soviet détente faced a major setback in 1979, when the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan.
The Soviet Union intended to support a client regime in Afghanistan, which the United States viewed as an act of expansion.
America placed an embargo on the shipment of American grain to the Soviets.

cards.title: Gorbachev's perestroika (and glasnost), step by step
body: **Step 1 – the crisis.** By 1980 the Soviet Union had a declining economy, rising infant mortality and poor working conditions. A small group of reformers appeared in the Communist Party.
**Step 2 – Gorbachev.** In **March 1985** Mikhail Gorbachev became leader and preached reform from the start.

**Step 3 – perestroika means "restructuring".** At first it meant restructuring the economy towards a **market economy** in which consumers influence what is produced, with limited free enterprise and some private property.

**Step 4 – political reform followed.** Gorbachev saw that economic reform was impossible without political reform. In **1988** he created an elected parliament, the **Congress of People's Deputies** (it met in 1989). In early **1990** he allowed non-communist parties and removed the Communist Party's guaranteed leading role from the constitution.
**Step 5 – result.** These reforms released forces that the party could not control and led to the end of the Soviet Union in 1991.
**Memory trick:** "Perestroika = Pieces rebuilt (restructuring); Glasnost = Glass (openness)."
**Exam tip:** Do not translate perestroika as "openness" – that is glasnost.

cards.title: Model answer: the end of détente
cards.problem: (Short answer) Explain why détente broke down in 1979.

steps.text: Define détente: the 1970s phase of relaxed tension and better relations between the superpowers.
Trigger: in 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan to support a client regime.
US view: the USA saw it as an act of Soviet expansion.

cards.answer: The 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, seen by the USA as expansion, ended détente; the USA answered with a grain embargo and confrontation returned.

lessons.title: Science and Technology during the Cold War

cards.title: 1.6 Science and Technology during the Cold War
body: Scientific and technological achievements since World War II have revolutionized people’s lives.
During the war, many scientists were recruited by governments to develop new weapons and other instruments of war.
The most famous product of wartime scientific research was the atomic bomb, created by a team of American and European scientists.
Most wartime devices, like the atomic bomb, were created for destructive purposes.
Computers and jet airplanes, however, show how wartime technology can easily be adapted for peacetime uses.

cards.title: How war research changed science, and how to spot bias in Cold War sources
body: **From war to peace.** Governments recruited scientists in WWII to make weapons. The atomic bomb was the most famous result, but **computers** and **jet aircraft** show how wartime technology was adapted for peaceful use.
**"Big science".** Wartime projects needed big teams, huge laboratories and expensive equipment that only governments and large corporations could pay for, and this became the new model for research.
**The space race.** The USSR launched **Sputnik I in 1957**; twelve years later, in **1969**, the USA landed astronauts on the Moon.

**Skill – checking a source for bias.** Ask: Which words make one side sound good or bad? Which facts are included and which are left out? What is exaggerated? Why was the source made, and does the author have a reason to be one-sided or to impress a certain audience?
**Exam tip:** Truman's 1947 speech or a Soviet statement will always show its own side's view – name the loaded words to prove bias.
**Memory trick:** "Bomb → Computer → Sputnik (1957) → Moon (1969)."

cards.title: Model answer: science and the Cold War
cards.problem: (Short answer) How did the world wars and the Cold War change science and technology?

steps.text: Governments recruited scientists during the war to develop new weapons and instruments of war.
The most famous result was the atomic bomb (American and European scientists), made for destruction.
The arms race continued it: A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles.

cards.answer: War and the arms race drove research (atomic bomb, missiles), but the same technology – computers, jet airplanes – was adapted for peaceful uses.

tips.text: The world from just the end of the Second World War up to 1990 was dominated by what was called the 'Cold War’.
Unlike the active conflict of the Second World War, the Cold War was a long period of tension and hostility that only occasionally broke out into open warfare.
This tension was caused by rivalry between the two superpowers that emerged after the end of the Second World War— the United States and the Soviet Union.
Underlying this rivalry were the ideological divisions between the two superpowers.
The United States was a capitalist liberal democracy.
The Soviet Union, on the other hand, was a oneparty socialist state. Each power tried to influence other nations to support its own way of life.
After 1945, a division emerged between the capitalist West (the US and Western Europe); and the socialist states (the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, and after 1949, China).
Both the US and the Soviet Union tried to influence the newly independent states in Africa and Asia.
On several occasions this caused open conflicts.
The prominent examples of such conflicts were Vietnam War (1960-75) and Angolan Civil War (1975-79).
Sticky wall: 1947 Truman + Marshall 1949 NATO · 1955 Warsaw 1961 Wall · 1962 Cuba 1989–91 endgame
It goes global · Alliances: NATO in the west. Warsaw Pact in the east. Arms race: A-bomb, then H-bomb, then missiles.
Berlin Wall 1961: East Germany seals the border to stop people leaving. Concrete symbol of the split until 1989.
Korea 1950–53: North (backed by USSR/China) vs South (UN/US). Ends near the 38th parallel. UN action happened while the USSR was boycotting the Security Council.
Cuba 1962: Soviet missiles on the island. Closest brush with nuclear war. Deal: missiles out of Cuba; later US missiles out of Turkey; promise not to invade Cuba.
Vietnam: Domino theory: if one state falls, neighbours follow. Long US war, huge anti-war movement at home, communist victory in 1975.
